interactions.title: Gnaeus agrees to share his research
lines: Kenzo: We're interested in your research.

Kenzo: Quite the opposite. Kenzo walks over, extends his hand. Kenzo from Dunmar. We are quite curious about your work from 20 years ago about a group of worshippers in the forest. Of the old hero of the Great War, right?
DM: Why would you want to bring up that painful time? He looks over at the students and says, go, go, class is over for today.
Wellby: Wellby pops up and says as the last student bursts out of the room, because we're headed upriver and we want to know what we're getting into.
DM: It's been a long time. Put that behind me. Even if the rest of the world won't.
Delwath: Um quick. We know why he's a... Why did we... Do we know some background? Am I forgetting some background here? Is this...

DM: Oh, he was accused of using enchantment magic to trick his subjects into talking to him. Discredited. And therefore, he was like a [garbled]... I mean, off... I was like, he was a very promising young scholar until he tricked his subjects into talking with enchantment magic, which is outlawed in Chardon, right.
Delwath: So, so the theory is nobody believes that nobody believes what he said they think it was all just kind of made up.

DM: Nobody believes that, and the book, only a few copies were ever written, which is why Dunmar only got, only got a copy recently, even though it's written 20 years ago. And he was discredited and never appointed to any to the Faculty in history and ended up as an undergraduate tutor with clearly not a very popular classes and clearly not a very prestigious college.

Delwath: ((Academic aside)) Delwath will say that the news of the new news of your travels has only reached some parts of the world recently. In Dunmar, for example, we only recently heard of this, of this tale, and I think you'll find that not everybody has the same reaction that the folks here in Chardon may have had. Some of us believe that what you saw was real.
DM: So why? Do you have power here? Can you change this? He waves his hand around the now empty room.

Kenzo: Well, one thing we can do we're going to forest that you described in your research and we want to learn what we can from you, and we can bring back perhaps evidence that can exonerate you then.
Kenzo: Would love your help, and we would love to learn more about your work.
DM: He he looks around. He looks over at Delwath, says... I am reluctant to bring up those old wounds but you would vouch for me, maybe, and now. The true history of these people. A letter, perhaps.

Delwath: And then I will be fine, I would be glad to provide whatever written support, I could based on our findings. It is a quite believable to us that Rai might be working in the woods somewhere given some stories we've heard or even visions we've seen.

DM: You misunderstand. Although. I would that part of my life has gone. I am curious. I have never given. I've never forgotten that journey, but if you were to write a letter vouching for my skill as a tutor from an Elf. The quality of students here would improve quite a bit.

Delwath: I understand now. I apologize for misunderstanding your needs. Of course, that would be something we could do. Perhaps, perhaps a working lunch, where you present your brilliant skills as a lecturer telling us all about your your journey and we will then write a glowing review.
DM: That as long as you're buying that sounds fine to me. Come. Let's go, there's a quiet place around the corner.
DM: So he takes you around the corner and you settle into... It's, it's like two in the afternoon and so it's a... There's not that many people there, um, he orders two lunches.

before: DM: In the middle of the oldest part of Chardon, the spire of the great... The spire of the Great Library stretches more than 700 feet, twisting into the air. From its lofty heights where you can see many of the smaller towers, the scattered halls and colleges that make up the university laid out, one might even imagine the long history of this place from the founding of the Great Library nearly 1000 years ago, to the growth of the university after the fall of Drankor or the founding of the Council of Magic, the Hetaeri Magica, to help regulate magical training and the growing academy; and finally, in the loss and pain after the Great War, the founding of the Society of the Open Scroll to preserve and protect magical and esoteric knowledge in the aftermath of that devastation.

From the lofty heights of the spire the bustle of students, faculty, tutors and others coming and going from the University proceeds over these layers of history, and into this activity come five adventurers, notable as it's rare to see an elf traveling with two dwarves, a halfling and a human these days. They have had a productive time in Chardon so far, learning that one of the artifacts they seek, the chalice of the rune priests, is now possessed by a man named Galen on the Faculty of Magic, a dabbler in the dangerous business of experimental metaphysics. The other, Eye of the Storm Giant Hralgar, seems to be in the keeping of a man named Fausto, one of the rich patrons of many expeditions, although no one can seem to agree how he got his wealth.

As you leave the Chapter House, a quiet student tavern, and head towards the nearest hall so you can connect with the disgraced tutor named Gnaeus, who knows something of the mysterious people in the forest to the east. A young dwarven student, barely past his caste ceremony, takes pity on you and leads you to Sibyl's Hall. Sibyl's Hall is one of the original colleges of the university. Although for a long time it was one of the most powerful and famous of the colleges that make up the University of Chardon, and since the Great War and the rise of the imperial power influence of many of the ancient religious orders has diminished. And so too has their wealth and power and the upkeep and prestige of the colleges they have supported.

The dwarven student leads you to a small lecture room in an ancient building now in need of extensive repairs. At the front of the room, a disheveled man, maybe in his 40s, scraggly black hair tied back, in need of a shave, with a gaunt, hungry look in his eyes, is reading desultorily from a text on logic to four students in the room. But as you enter and the dwarf, the young dwarf scurries away, he slowly trails off to nothing and turns to stare at you. This man is apparently... looks up and says, aggravated and glancing over your armor and your traveling cloaks and clear signs of if not extravagant wealth, at least power and skill. “Well, why are you disturbing my meager lessons? What do such clearly powerful men and women want with me?”

interactions.title: Gnaeus recounts the forest tribes and the hidden god
lines: DM: ((Gnaeus’s appearance)) So, as he, as he eats for a minute, he kind of sighs. This is 25 years ago. I grew up. So I grew up in Arendum near the Crimson Forest in the Elderwood and I... You know, I was always curious.

The Baz'aku, a tribe of the Deno'qai people, would come trade and, you know, they claimed anyway, the stories they told was how they were the first people to settle Taelgar. They lived in these woods since the empires of the elves. So when I came to Chardon and studied history, it was, it was natural that I would... I would want to go back and see what was true and what was myth. So much was lost in the wars, though. You know, the battles against hobgoblins and trolls and when the dragons attacked drove back the Chard- Chardonian forces across the Chasa. Devastating Battle of Shadowfire close to Chardon. Nobody's ever really ventured back into the woods after that. Was 150 years ago almost 200 years ago now. There's stories of course.

So I went to the Elderwood, went up the Kayan River, spent six months at the Baz'aku, earning their trust, learning about their way of life and you know, how they lived in the eaves of the Elderwood, the myths of the Deno'qai, the people of the gods in their tongue. Supposedly, the first humans to leave Hkar long before the Downfall. They claim that there were once forests that stretched from Dunmar, the deserts now to the south, all the way north beyond the edge of the of the Chardonian Empire before the Downfall. They said their people remembered even beyond, far north as the land of fire and ice where the sun never sets in summer.
Delwath: Those claims are true. The elves also remember.
DM: Of course, he would. So I spoke with them. I learned a little bit of their worship of the tanshi, the spirits of the forest that bring their prayers to Anida, our creator.
Delwath: Hey Tim, is Anida the same word for the creator that Aaviskar used? Yep.
DM: From them, I learned of stranger things in the heart of the forest, the Elderwood, the oldest and the most intact of these ancient forests.

DM: Okay. I'm. So Gnaeus continues. I convinced one of them, Baz’aku, to take me south across the Chasa. Spent two years living with another tribe. They taught me more about the tanshi, about the small sacrifices that bring prayers and magic. They taught me about their history. How their people had once stretched for a thousand miles or more, north and south.

DM: Um, great. He pauses for a moment. I wanted to find what was at the heart of the forest. I thought that would make my name. And I guess that turned to be my downfall. Because none would take me. They said ruins of elven cities hidden in the trees, scars cut across the land by some evil where trees no longer grow, haunted battlefields where the restless spirits of Deno'qai and Chardonians and elves alike fought against hobgoblins and trolls and even dragons in endless battle.

DM: So that's like that's like like north of the river, and this is like south of the river is that... Whether they were... So Gnaeus continues. Whether they were scared or cautious or just distrusted me, none would guide me. So I resorted to magic. I brought with me some chalyte spells. And I used one to charm a guide to compel cooperation for 30 days and asked him to lead me to the tribe, the people who lived at the heart of the Elderwood near the source of the Kayan River. I never. Nothing I recorded, no stories I brought back were ever compelled. Simply the cooperation of a guide. But when that enchantment wore off, they turned on me. And I fled. And rumors spread among the Deno'qai. Gnaeus the charmer, Gnaeus the cursed one.

Those stories got back to Chardon. But I learned from Jordo, the god-caller at that time, that the... The people there who lived in the at the source of the Kayan, they call themselves the Te'kula. Only worship one god, not like the other tribes who worship many small spirits. This spirit, they called... They called Rai. They also referred to them as or believed or what Jordo told me was that there was a great tree there, had fallen in the deepest part of the woods and the god, the old god of the Elderwood, the spirit that had been destroyed, the spirit of the ancient great trees that was thought to have been lost when their ancestors were driven from their homelands in the Elderwood during the, the wars right after the fall of Cha'mutte, had come back, had been revived in this tree. Now calling himself Rai instead of simply his old name. Jordo said that Rai or Aasimti spoke with him through dreams. There was something there was a... The heart of the tree they call that something they found some physical object from this tree. That when the god-caller possessed that would allow Rai to speak some through some magic or prayer to them in their dreams. And this god, Rai or Aasimti has kept the Te'kula safe for several generations now I guess longer had been... It had been three generations when I spoke with Jordo, and it's been 25 years since. There was some evil, they would not speak of something that lurked in the woods, that saying, speaking its name summoned it, and that even...
Rai or he could not keep them safe if it was summoned, but while he was there, he kept them hidden.

DM: Aasimti protected their tribe, protected their village and their homeland. This evil thing they said dwelt in the east, and it first came to their lands in disguise. Soon after Aasimti was restored, speaking with honeyed tongue and asking for Rai’s spirit, for Aasimti’s spirit, asking for the heart of the tree. And then threatening utter destruction when it was refused. And their myth tells them, it was only a desperate prayer to Aasimti to try to hide them kept... That kept them alive from this creature, and now they say the power of Rai keeps them hidden from the world.
Kenzo: Have you seen this tree?
DM: They would not allow outsiders to see it. Even with my charm the guide could not take me.
Delwath: With you... Was finding the way difficult without a guide? Could you... Did you draw a map if we wanted to return to this village?
DM: I'm not sure it was possible with Rai's protections around this tribe.
Delwath: Where did you find the guide?

DM: There's many tribes of Deno'qai that live in the forest. As I said, I I charmed one of the one of the people of the of another tribe, Bek'eni, to take me. They of course the Te'kula are not totally isolated. They have commerce and trade with other Deno'qai tribes. But it seems without a guide... No outsider can find them. And no guide would take me.
Kenzo: What do you think the guides were looking for in order to take someone?
DM: If they were Deno'qai. They might take an elf, I guess. Your homeland, too long ago.
Kenzo: And the Deno'qai or, I, sorry, sorry if I missed this, the Deno'qai, are they, are they elves or are they humans?

DM: They're, they're humans. They call themselves the first people. The people of the gods. They say they came to Taelgar when the elves still ruled the forests. They came to this land from Hkar, where humans were born, and they were the first to set foot outside of Hkar.
Seeker: With what kind of a life do those villagers lead, lead deep in that forest?
DM: They raise pigs. They wrestle they climb trees. They grow some some crops.
Seeker: Did they clear the forest and make houses?
DM: Yeah, I wouldn't say they clear forest. They live among the trees, but yes, there is a village.
Seeker: And do they use the waterways? They go about in boats up and down?
DM: Some do. The the Te'kula live... Far from any navigable streams.
Delwath: Perhaps you could at least tell us how to get to the village where you found a guide. Or is that just any village?
DM: Upriver, that is not hard. I I simply follow the the Kayan River. Till I found a village. I don't know if they're... I don't know how long they maintain a village if they migrate.
Delwath: But there are many peoples along the Kayan River.
Delwath: And, and the peoples along the Kayan River, they, they worship the... What was the name he used for the small gods?
DM: Yeah many of them seemed like they had hundreds of gods.
Delwath: And are they newly settled, are there any refugees from further north amongst them in their stories.
DM: There may be, I mean they they tell of an exodus and return. They only returned to these...
DM: Now six generations ago, maybe hardly more than a century.
Delwath: And have... Do you know if folks have left the southern, the Elderwood for the Crimson Wood and returned to their homelands? Are the.

DM: The... I do not know. I know the what I learned from the people I spoke with was that there are... There are Deno'qai people living... Along the edges of the Chardonian Empire as far north as Voltara and beyond. But the further north you go, the more the tribes suffered in the blood. And the ancient communication networks have been disrupted as the forests have been cut and destroyed by battle and fire.
Seeker: What made up those networks?
Seeker: I want to try to ask using our in character, knowledge of stories of Dimitar if if this guy knows anything about that it would be like. A small winged lizard. With a sharp tongue.
Unknown: Like, is there anything in the lore?
Delwath: Did did this God, I mean we just ask if. This God if there's any stories of this God having companions.
DM: The god-caller would not share the contents of his dreams with me.
DM: They did not speak much to outsiders.
Delwath: How. Was the god-caller a position passed from generation to generation?
DM: It is it is like the it's like the head priest, I gather. And is the one who manages the relationship with the tanshi and...
Delwath: And the one you spoke to was old, young?
DM: He was old when I spoke. He was he was younger when he found a heart of this tree. It had been several generations past when they returned to those woods.
Kenzo: Did they say what the heart of the tree look like?

DM: I only got a glimpse once. The god-caller wore it around his neck under his shirt. It was green and smooth and looked looked like it was encased in bark though it was encased in some wooden structure, and there was some sort of... The heart itself under there seems to be something green. But he would never show it to me.
Kenzo: Well what's his name again? Jordo, Jordo.
DM: And I suspect he is dead by now. He was already old 25 years ago.
Kenzo: Hmm, did Jordo say how he came across this stone?

DM: Found it. He didn't call it a stone, he called it the heart of the tree. That great tree had fallen, a huge tree, maybe hundred feet or more tall 200 feet tall. And the legend is the heart restored the god, the spirit of the Elderwood to life. And now the life of Aasimti, the spirit of the Elderwood, now calling himself Rai... Was encased within this tree or the heart of this tree.
Delwath: Kenzo, are you thinking there might be a piece of jade inside there?
Kenzo: Coming up, of course, that it is a piece of jade.

Delwath: Would you be able to... This, um... These stories are fascinating and revealing and I think we are quite likely to be heading that way soon. Would you be able to to to write down the names and faces of the people you remember?
DM: I will give you a copy of my book, nobody else seems to want to.
Kenzo: Love a copy of your book.
Seeker: Look, did Jordo have an apprentice, someone we might expect to meet?
DM: Did not know how the god-caller was passed from generation to generation.
DM: I believe they were chosen by the spirits, or at least that is what the Deno'qai believe.
Kenzo: What was his name again? Jordo, Jordo.
Kenzo: How much time did you spend with Jordo?

DM: Remember, I was only there for less than 30 days when my enchantment on the guy on my guide wore off and he realized he had been charmed. He revealed to everybody, what I had done and I was driven at spear point out of the village. I'm surprised I escaped with my life. So I did not have a long time to get to know anybody there.
Kenzo: Did you have a sense of how the how they were organized? Was Jordo the, the leader? Was there... You know, a sense of the culture and the structure of their society.

DM: There was a... They seem to have this was not a very big village remember. But it seemed that they had a chief. An elder who was chosen by the people of the village. Chief. Not Jordo. The god-caller was separate. They had. [garbled] When there were decisions to be made such as when they were deciding my punishment, it seemed that there were many of them gathered together and spoke and debated.

DM: He, he clearly could do some magic.
DM: He would do small prayers, he would heal people's wounds.
DM: Never took it out. Remember, he always had it close to him.
Kenzo: Can you say again what what the stone did, or what he claimed it did?

DM: Claimed it gave him dreams. That the god Rai or formerly the god, the tanshi Aasimti, the spirit of this forest, spoke to him in his dreams. Told him, out to give him warnings about what was happening and some stranger visions that he could not interpret. And then. This god, the spirit, protected the village, hid it somehow from this evil they would not name that came to try and steal the heart of this world.
